name: Karl Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, parties or government. This is confidential. Tell me about a normal day on your shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the complaint-call shift at a contact centre. I have a two-year college diploma, but most of my skill came from listening through long billing disputes. I earn well for this job and like getting a caller a plain answer. I don't use the AI reply box; I'd rather read the account and speak for myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What gives you breathing room outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have saved about eight months of expenses, and there are several other centres around town. That helps, though I don't spend the money casually. I want to keep a job I know how to do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my shift the old telephone skills still matter. A machine can fill in a simple form, but it cannot hear when a caller is ashamed to ask again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm comfortable with my place here. I earn well for this work, have eight months of expenses saved with my partner, and could try another centre nearby if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep handling complaint calls and reviewing the team's handwritten case notes. During the first year I'll keep our savings untouched and ask for the same lead rota rather than change a system that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'm glad the big claims amount to little, and ordinary work still pays the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the reply box yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't use the AI reply box. My colleague tests it, and I read the customer record directly when a case comes to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the reserve for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I keep that reserve for a genuine loss of work. We would not spend it just because a vendor promises a better headset.

say: I'd say **telephone skills** still settle difficult cases.
I'd let simple forms change while keeping **human listening** on the line.
think: I feel **secure** in my lead post and good pay.
Our **eight-month reserve** and nearby centres give me a fallback.
do: Keep handling **complaint calls** on my usual lead rota throughout the first year.
Review the team's **case notes** without using AI.
feel: **Calm** because work and household money look secure.
S0.quote: A machine can fill in a simple form, but it cannot hear when a caller is ashamed to ask again.
fieldNote: He trusts **direct listening** and has never used the AI reply box.
His **high pay** and long reserve support a steady course.
He sees **nearby centres** as a practical fallback, not an urgent move.

steps.text: Keep handling complaint calls on his regular lead rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say management should tell us when it stops replacing agents. If the easy chats leave, the hard calls won't get shorter just because there are fewer staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect my lead pay makes me a target even though I settle the worst complaints. Eight months saved and plenty of local centres give me time, but I dislike having my work measured by a bot I won't use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the next staff meeting I'll ask for the planned headcount and call-time rules with two other leads. If my hours are cut in the first year, I'll contact nearby centres about posted lead vacancies with wages close to mine; until then I'll stay on my present shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I can cover a gap. I don't like a quiet change to the rules when my higher pay may put my job at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would ask about headcount with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for the plan in writing so every shift hears the same number. I won't ask a junior agent to take a stand alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you search first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the customer desk at the station across town first. They posted a lead vacancy last spring, but I would check the present wage before applying.

say: I'd request **headcount plans** before the centre stops replacing staff.
I'd argue **hard calls** need realistic time targets.
think: I worry my **higher lead pay** could make me a target.
I can use **eight months saved** and nearby centres if hours fall.
do: Ask with **two leads** for written staffing and call-time rules.
Stay on my **present shift** while hours remain.
Apply for a **posted nearby lead job** only if hours fall and wages stay close to my current pay.
feel: **Anxious** about my own job despite savings that could cover a gap.
S1.quote: If the easy chats leave, the hard calls won't get shorter just because there are fewer staff.
fieldNote: He opposes **quiet staffing cuts** rather than software in the abstract.
His **group request** protects junior agents from standing alone.
A **wage check** precedes any move to a nearby centre.

steps.text: Ask with two leads for written headcount plans
Keep working his present lead shift while hours remain
Apply for posted nearby lead vacancies if hours fall and wages stay close to current pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to get the notice terms now if general AI can do calls by 2028. Robots around 2031 come too late to matter for people at headsets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job could go despite my record. Eight months of expenses gives my partner and me a start, but if all the nearby centres replace calls at once, the old route to another desk closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll put my contract and performance letters in one folder and ask, with the other leads, for written notice terms. If the centre removes my post in the first year after 2028, I'll look for posted paid complaint-mediation work outside call centres and take a job only when its wage covers our share of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have money for a search, but I don't have a trade ready to step into overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of opening would you search for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first check the public complaint office's current postings, not an old advert. If nothing is open, I will keep searching while we draw on the reserve for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner we can cover eight months at current spending, then agree a lower monthly budget if the dismissal actually comes. I won't pretend that reserve lasts forever.

say: I'd ask for **written notice** before 2028 changes call jobs.
I'd tell agents **2031 robots** offer no delay to telephone work.
think: I expect my **lead post** could disappear.
I fear **nearby call jobs** might close together despite eight months saved.
do: Ask with **other leads** for written notice terms now.
Seek **posted paid mediation work** after an actual dismissal.
Set a **lower household budget** if my wages stop.
feel: **Anxious** because the reserve buys time, not another trade.
S2.quote: Eight months of expenses gives my partner and me a start, but if all the nearby centres replace calls at once, the old route to another desk closes.
fieldNote: His **cash reserve** does not solve a field-wide loss of work.
He insists on **current postings** and a wage that covers bills.
He remains **technology resistant** even under a fast change.

steps.text: Ask with other leads for written dismissal notice terms
Apply for posted paid mediation vacancies after dismissal if wages cover bills
Lower household spending after an actual loss of wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff five years gives the centre time to say which jobs it will keep. I would still watch 2031 for our calls, not 2034 for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine moving to a complaints desk before general AI arrives, but I don't want to leave higher pay for a guess. My partner and I can compare openings calmly while I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll visit the public complaint office and ask what its desk pays and what qualifications it actually requires. If a posted paid vacancy appears before 2031 at a wage that covers our bills, I'll apply; in the first year after AGI I'll stay in whichever paid role I hold while checking new posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though I can breathe. Five years makes the search less like a fire drill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the complaints office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the office manager examples of disputes I settled, with customer names removed. I would not enrol in a course unless a job posting required it and I knew the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I still wouldn't use the AI reply box myself. I can learn a new desk's rules without handing my judgment to a screen.

say: I'd demand a **five-year job plan** from the centre.
I'd watch **2031 calls**, not the later 2034 robot date.
think: I might find a **complaints desk** before general AI arrives.
I won't leave **higher pay** for an unposted job.
do: Check **complaint-office pay** and requirements this year.
Apply only for a **posted paid vacancy** covering our bills.
Keep my **current paid role** while vacancies remain uncertain.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to plan without haste.
S3.quote: I can learn a new desk's rules without handing my judgment to a screen.
fieldNote: He will **investigate qualifications**, not pay for a speculative course.
His **wage floor** shapes any move away from the centre.
His refusal to **use AI** stays consistent as the timeline lengthens.

steps.text: Apply for posted paid complaint-office vacancies if wages cover bills
Keep his current paid shift while no suitable opening exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for employers to give people proper notice and for workers to choose where to go. Our calls still change in 2036, three years before hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 27, I can stay in work I understand for a good while and move only when a sound opening appears. I feel secure enough not to chase every prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the coming year I'll keep taking the complex calls and check the local complaint-office postings every six months. If general AI arrives in 2036, I'll use that first year to apply for a posted paid office role only if my centre hours fall and the new wage covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade gives me choice, and our savings let me refuse a poor offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What proof of skill would you show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a future interviewer the thank-you letters customers sent after disputed bills were fixed. Those letters say more about my work than a software certificate I do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will keep the reserve above six months of expenses, replacing what we use from pay. That lets us choose rather than accept the first low wage offered.

say: I'd expect **proper notice** over a decade, so workers can compare jobs before their current shifts change.
I'd distinguish **2036 call work** from robots arriving around 2039.
think: I can keep **familiar work** while the centre pays me well.
I feel **secure enough** to reject poor offers.
do: Handle **complex calls** during the coming year.
Check **paid complaint-office postings** twice yearly; apply only if hours fall and wages cover bills.
Maintain at least **six months** of expenses, replacing any reserve withdrawals from pay.
feel: **Calm** because time and savings preserve choice.
S4.quote: A decade gives me choice, and our savings let me refuse a poor offer.
fieldNote: He values **choice** more than speed in changing jobs.
His **customer letters** are the proof he trusts.
He maintains a **six-month floor** while waiting for a sound opening.

steps.text: Keep handling complex customer calls this year
Check paid complaint-office postings twice yearly; apply if centre hours fall and wages cover bills
Replenish savings used from pay while maintaining at least six months of expenses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Even nearby centres might stop hiring callers at the same time, and eight months of savings is not a replacement occupation. Written notice and real paid complaint-office vacancies would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who takes responsibility when a caller says the account record is wrong. People often know something the screen doesn't show. Someone should still have time to listen before declaring the case closed.

headlineQuote: Someone should still have time to listen before declaring the case closed.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old lead** at a contact centre, with a two-year college diploma and strong complaint-handling skill.
He earns **higher pay**, shares expenses with a partner and has eight months saved; many similar centres operate nearby.
He never uses **AI tools**, preferring account records, callers and written staffing terms over a new reply box.
The **2028 picture** worries him most; longer windows let him check paid complaint-office openings without leaving good wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close nearby call jobs together before he finds another kind of work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** would let his shift plan before hours disappear.
**Paid complaint-office openings** with enough wages would offer a realistic route.
